newsitem.title: KENYA: IMF official preaches better management for Kenya.
newsitem.headline: IMF official preaches better management for Kenya.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund official on Thursday called for better economic management in Kenya, regretting the bloated civil service, corruption, neglected infrastructure and poor marketing of tourism.

But Walter Mahler, ending his three-year tour of duty as IMF resident representative in Kenya, was encouraged by a variety of economic reforms in the period which cut inflation to a single digit from 101 percent in 1993 and reversed economic decline.

"This is just a country not running well. You've got to repair the obvious things -- collect the garbage, repair roads. For example, traffic lights on a major street in the city centre have not worked for three-and-a-half months. That is not rocket science," Mahler told a news briefing.
"You have to have a system of local government that works. It is clear that the present one doesn't," Mahler added.
Mahler said a little more imagination was required to sell Kenya as a tourist destination.

He said Kenya had relied on the same kind of tourist safaris for 25 years and required alternatives to parks and beaches. The Kenyan authorities had to put money into marketing if they expected a rise in tourist acitivity in the country.
Tourism is Kenya's leading foreign exchange earner.
Mahler said international donor countries and agencies, including the IMF and World Bank, had put corruption in Kenya firmly on their agendas and nothing would push that away.
"This is a serious concern. Kenya is going to have to significantly reduce it. There is no good counter-argument for it. The issue is not going to just go away," Mahler said.

But the IMF official also spoke out strongly against international companies that paid bribes to obtain favours, suggesting that American-type laws that made bribing a foreign official a criminal offence were required to end the practice.
Mahler said he looked to a future of a trimmed but well-paid civil service, saying better wages would be a major incentive against corruption for police and judicial officers.
He also wanted actions to end wastage in the health sector, where he saw poor equipment use, the oversupply of non-essential but expensive medicines and under-use of supplied medicines.
With general elections due some time in 1997, Mahler said fears that the economy would be run down as it was with the "unusual economic policies of 1992/93" had subsided.

In the 1992/93 period, the government printed money to win votes in landmark pluralist elections, sending inflation spiralling to a peak of 101 percent in October 1993 and the shilling to an all-time low of 84 versus the dollar.
Since then, Mahler said, prudent fiscal measures had been put in place and the central bank and the treasury had won praise all round for measures that encouraged economic growth.
Kenya's gross domestic product (GDP) growth is forecast to grow at around 5.5 percent in 1996, up from 4.9 percent in 1995.
Mahler's successor, Reimer Carstens, is already in Kenya.
An IMF mission headed by an assistant director in the African department, Hiroyuki Hino, is due in Kenya next week to assess Kenya's progress in meeting economic targets.
IMF blessing normally leads to other donors opening up their aid purses.
